syllabus.clause: checkpoint frequency trading recovery time against write amplification and full-page-write volume
the WAL as the substrate that physical replication, point-in-time recovery and logical decoding (CDC, Ch.8) are all built on

items.item: in the event of a crash, recovery looks at the latest checkpoint record to determine the redo record it should start REDO from

reducing checkpoint_timeout/max_wal_size causes checkpoints more often, allowing faster after-crash recovery at the cost of flushing dirty pages more often, and, with full_page_writes on, logging the entire page content on the first modification after each checkpoint
a crash can be recovered from using the log, redoing any changes not yet applied to data pages — roll-forward recovery, also known as REDO

at.step: Reveal: redo-only vs. ARIES's three passes

items.item: it is not necessary to replay WAL entries all the way to the end; replay can stop at any point and produce a consistent snapshot as of that time, which is point-in-time recovery
in standby mode, the server continuously applies WAL received from the primary, read from an archive or streamed directly over a TCP connection
logical decoding is implemented by decoding the contents of the write-ahead log into an application-specific form, such as a stream of tuples or SQL statements

sources.source: ARIES (Mohan et al. 1992) — named, not block-quoted (OCR unreliable)

items.item: ARIES makes three passes over the log — analysis, redo, and undo — undoing the updates of transactions still in progress ('losers') at crash time

at.step: Reveal: redo-only vs. ARIES's three passes

items.item: A checkpoint is a point in the transaction sequence where Postgres guarantees every dirty data page has actually been flushed to disk; crash recovery never needs to look further back than the most recent checkpoint's own redo record, per the WAL Configuration documentation.

Reducing checkpoint_timeout or max_wal_size makes checkpoints happen more often, which bounds how much WAL a crash recovery must replay, at the real cost of flushing dirty pages more often and, when full_page_writes is on (the default), logging a full copy of each page on its first change after every checkpoint — a real, documented trade-off, not a rule of thumb.

full_page_writes defends against a torn page (a page partly written when the OS or drive crashes mid-write) by logging the entire page content on the first real modification to that page after each checkpoint, so a checkpoint interval and the full-page-write volume are directly, mechanically linked, not independently tunable.

Postgres's own WAL documentation describes crash recovery as a single roll-forward operation (REDO) from the checkpoint's redo record; it never describes a separate pass that physically undoes an uncommitted transaction's changes, because a row's own transaction status (not an undo pass) decides whether it is visible.

at.step: Reveal: redo-only vs. ARIES's three passes

items.item: ARIES (Mohan et al., 1992) explicitly defines a third, separate pass — undo — that physically rolls back the updates of transactions that were still in progress ('losers') when the crash happened, a real, distinct recovery phase Postgres's own redo-only path never runs.

at.step: Reveal: redo-only vs. ARIES's three passes

items.item: This topic's own real measurement (examples.py) checkpoints a two-thousand-row table every round versus only once before ten identical rounds of the same update, and finds the frequent-checkpoint run logs roughly nineteen times as many full-page images (1267 vs 66) while keeping the real, measured replay distance to about a seventh of the infrequent run's (roughly 1.4 MB vs 9.6 MB) — the documented trade-off as a real, concrete number, not an abstract claim.

Point-in-time recovery works by replaying WAL only up to a chosen point rather than all the way to the end, per Postgres's own Continuous Archiving documentation; it is a direct, structural use of the identical WAL and checkpoint mechanism this topic measures, not a separate recovery system.

Physical replication ships the raw WAL bytes themselves to a standby, which continuously performs the identical REDO Postgres's own crash recovery does, just against a different, remote copy of the data files rather than its own — the same mechanism, applied continuously rather than only after a crash.

Logical decoding (the basis of change-data-capture pipelines, Data Engineering Ch.8) reads and decodes the identical WAL stream this topic measures into row-level changes, rather than raw bytes, so a consumer can replay a table's own changes without replaying Postgres's own internal page format at all.

pg_control_checkpoint()'s redo_lsn is exactly the point crash recovery would resume replay from if the server crashed right now; the gap between it and pg_current_wal_lsn() is a real, direct, live measurement of how much WAL a crash this instant would force a replay of, not an estimate.
